qaraqara-charka-confederation.t: A confederation of Aymara-speaking peoples in the southern Bolivian highlands, renowned as warriors and later linked to the silver mines of Potosí.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.o: In the centuries after Tiwanaku's collapse, the Qaraqara and Charka formed a federation of peoples in the southern highlands of modern Bolivia, around Potosí and Chuquisaca, around 1200. The federation included groups such as the Chuy and Chicha.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.r: The confederation was organised in two halves led by the Qaraqara in the south and the Charka in the north, each under hereditary lords. It is known chiefly from a memorial written by its lords in 1582, which describes their service as soldiers for the Incas. The peoples herded llamas, farmed tubers and maize, and worked silver and other metals.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.e: The confederation came under Inca rule around 1460 and served the Incas in war. After the Spanish conquest, its lands formed the core of the Royal Audiencia of Charcas, and the silver mountain of Potosí, discovered in 1545, lay in Qaraqara territory.

qajar-iran.t: The Turkmen-origin dynasty that ruled Iran from Tehran through its loss of the Caucasus, Great Power rivalry and the Constitutional Revolution of 1906.
qajar-iran.o: Agha Mohammad Khan, chief of the Qajar tribe, fought the Zand dynasty after Karim Khan's death in 1779. He made Tehran his capital in 1786, defeated the last Zand ruler Lotf Ali Khan in 1794, sacked Tiflis in 1795 and was crowned shah in 1796. He was assassinated in 1797, and his nephew Fath Ali Shah succeeded.
qajar-iran.r: Fath Ali Shah lost the Caucasus to the Russian Empire by the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828). Under Naser al-Din Shah (1848 to 1896) the minister Amir Kabir founded the Dar ol-Fonun college, but the shahs relied on foreign loans and concessions, provoking the tobacco protest of 1891 to 1892. The Constitutional Revolution created a parliament (Majlis) in 1906, while the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 divided Iran into spheres of influence.
qajar-iran.e: After occupation in the First World War, Reza Khan seized power in a 1921 coup. In 1925 the Majlis deposed Ahmad Shah, ending the dynasty, and made Reza Khan shah, founding Pahlavi Iran.

qi-1130-1137.t: A Jurchen client state in Henan and Shaanxi under the former Song official Liu Yu, used as a buffer and spearhead against the Southern Song.
qi-1130-1137.o: Liu Yu, Song prefect of Jinan, surrendered to the Jurchen in 1128. In 1130 the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) installed him as emperor of Great Qi to govern the conquered lands south of the Yellow River, first from Daming and from 1132 from Kaifeng.
qi-1130-1137.r: Liu Yu ruled with Chinese-style institutions but imposed heavy taxes and labour to pay for war. With Jin support his armies attacked Southern Song several times between 1133 and 1136, but were defeated by Song generals including Yue Fei, and Qi lost credibility with its masters.
qi-1130-1137.e: In 1137 the Jin court abolished Qi, demoted Liu Yu to a prince and took the territory under direct rule. Its lands were briefly returned to the Song in a treaty of 1139 before the Jurchen reoccupied them in 1140.

qwabe-chiefdom.t: A northern Nguni chiefdom, senior kin of the Zulu, that was conquered and absorbed by Shaka around 1818.
qwabe-chiefdom.o: Tradition holds that Qwabe and Zulu were sons of Malandela, and the Qwabe line was originally the larger and more senior. By the 18th century the Qwabe were settled near the lower Mhlathuze river in what is now KwaZulu-Natal.
qwabe-chiefdom.r: Qwabe chiefs ruled cattle-herding homesteads through royal kin and councillors, and their lineage claimed ritual seniority over the Zulu. Under Kondlo and later Phakathwayo, the chiefdom was among the significant powers south of the Mthethwa Paramountcy.
qwabe-chiefdom.e: Around 1818 Shaka defeated Phakathwayo, who died soon after, and the Qwabe were incorporated into the Zulu Kingdom, providing many of its soldiers and notables. Some Qwabe later broke away under Nqetho in 1829.

que.t: Que, a Neo-Hittite kingdom of the Cilician plain around Adana, known for its horses and for bilingual inscriptions in Luwian and Phoenician.
que.o: After the Hittite collapse, a kingdom arose in the fertile Cilician plain, formerly Kizzuwatna. Its people called it Hiyawa, a name some link with the Greek Ahhiyawa, and its capital was Adana. Assyrian texts call it Que from the 9th century BCE.
que.r: Kings such as Awariku, the Urikki of Assyrian texts, ruled with Phoenician as a prestige language beside Luwian; bilingual inscriptions at Karatepe and Çineköy are key to deciphering Luwian hieroglyphs. Que bred horses, which the Bible says Solomon bought there.
que.e: Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire campaigned against King Kate. Urikki became a vassal of Tiglath-Pileser III, and by 713 BCE Sargon II had made Que an Assyrian province.

quaiti-sultanate.t: The richest of the Hadrami sultanates, founded with money earned in Indian service and ruled from the port of Mukalla.
quaiti-sultanate.o: The Qu'aiti were a Yafa'i family whose head, Umar ibn Awad al-Qu'aiti, rose to high rank as a commander in the army of the Nizam of Hyderabad. With Indian wealth they bought land and influence in Hadramawt, taking Shibam and the port of Shihr from around 1858, then Mukalla from the Kasadi Sultanate in 1881.
quaiti-sultanate.r: Mukalla became the capital, with a palace, customs house and modern administration; the sultans long spent much time in Hyderabad. Treaties with Britain from 1882 made the state part of the Aden Protectorate, later the Eastern Aden Protectorate, and the Kathiri-Qu'aiti agreement of 1918 settled relations with the Kathiri Sultanate. Remittances from Southeast Asia and the Hadhrami Bedouin Legion sustained the state.
quaiti-sultanate.e: In September 1967 the National Liberation Front seized Mukalla while the young sultan Ghalib ibn Awad al-Qu'aiti was abroad, and the sultanate was abolished within South Yemen.

qin-xue-ju.t: A short-lived rebel empire in Gansu whose armies briefly beat the young Tang but were destroyed by Li Shimin in 618.
qin-xue-ju.o: Xue Ju, a rich and powerful man of Jincheng (modern Lanzhou), rose in revolt in 617 as the Sui Dynasty disintegrated. He took the title Hegemon-King of Western Qin, then proclaimed himself emperor of Qin and moved his capital east to Tianshui, threatening the Wei valley around Chang'an.
qin-xue-ju.r: The regime was essentially a military confederation of Gansu frontier troops, known for their harsh treatment of captives, and Xue Ju appointed relatives and generals to the main offices rather than building a civil administration. Its aim was to take Chang'an itself. In 618 its army defeated Tang forces under Li Shimin at Qianshuiyuan, when Li Shimin was ill.
qin-xue-ju.e: Xue Ju died soon after this victory, and his son Xue Rengao succeeded him. Later in 618 Li Shimin returned, wore down the Qin army and routed it at Qianshuiyuan; Xue Rengao surrendered and was executed in Chang'an, opening the north-west to the Tang Dynasty.

qasimid-state.t: The Zaydi imamate that drove the Ottomans out of Yemen in 1636 and briefly united the country while Mocha coffee reached Europe.
qasimid-state.o: In 1597 al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, a Zaydi scholar, proclaimed himself imam and began a revolt against Yemen Eyalet from the northern mountains. His son al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad continued the war until the Ottoman Empire evacuated Yemen in 1636, leaving the Qasimid family masters of the country.
qasimid-state.r: Under al-Mutawakkil Isma'il, imam from 1644 to 1676, the state reached its greatest extent, taking Aden, Lahej and Hadramawt. Its wealth came from coffee, shipped through Mocha to Cairo and, through Dutch, English and French factories, to Europe. Although Zaydi doctrine called for elected imams, succession became dynastic, and the court at Sanaa or al-Mawahib resembled a monarchy.
qasimid-state.e: From the early 18th century southern and eastern districts broke away, including the Sultanate of Lahej, and coffee exports fell as colonial plantations grew. Rival imams, tribal revolts and Wahhabi raids weakened it further. In 1872 the Ottomans took Sanaa and formed the Yemen Vilayet.

qara-qoyunlu.t: A Turkmen confederation, the 'Black Sheep', that ruled Azerbaijan, Iraq and much of Iran in the 15th century until defeated by the rival White Sheep.
qara-qoyunlu.o: The Qara Qoyunlu were Oghuz Turkmen tribes of the region around Lake Van and Mosul. Their leader Bayram Khwaja emerged in the 1370s as a vassal of the Jalayirids. Qara Yusuf fought Timur, fled to the Mamluk Sultanate, returned after Timur's death and in 1410 defeated and killed Ahmad Jalayir, taking Tabriz and Baghdad.
qara-qoyunlu.r: The confederation was ruled by the Qara Yusuf family through tribal leaders and Persian officials, with Tabriz as capital. Iskandar fought the Timurid Shah Rukh. Jahan Shah (1438 to 1467) expanded the state to its greatest extent, briefly taking Herat in 1458, and wrote poetry in Turkic and Persian; the Blue Mosque of Tabriz was built in his reign. The dynasty has been associated with Shia sympathies, though this is debated.
qara-qoyunlu.e: In 1467 Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu defeated and killed Jahan Shah. His son Hasan Ali was defeated in 1468, and Aq Qoyunlu absorbed the state.

qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Qara Khitai origin that ruled Kerman under Mongol overlordship and produced two notable women rulers.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.o: Baraq Hajib, an officer of Qara Khitai origin who had served the Khwarazmian Empire, seized Kerman in 1222 during the chaos of the Mongol invasions. He submitted to the Mongols and received the title Qutlugh Khan, which gave the dynasty its name.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.r: The Qutlugh-Khanids ruled Kerman as vassals first of the Great Khans and then of the Ilkhanate, keeping the province prosperous through trade with the Gulf. Qutlugh Terken Khatun, widow of Qutb al-Din Muhammad, governed from 1257 to 1282 and was remembered for justice, irrigation works and building. Her daughter Padishah Khatun, wife successively of the Ilkhans Abaqa and Gaykhatu, ruled Kerman from 1292 but was executed in 1295.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.e: Family rivalries and Ilkhanid intervention weakened the dynasty. In 1306 the Ilkhan Öljeitü ended its rule and placed Kerman under appointed governors.

qi-206-bc.t: The revived kingdom of Qi in Shandong, fought over by the Tian clan, Xiang Yu and Han Xin during the Chu-Han war, until Han Xin made himself its king in 203 BCE.
qi-206-bc.o: In 206 BCE Xiang Yu split the old State of Qi into three, making the Qi general Tian Du King of Qi at Linzi. Tian Rong, the clan strongman left out of the settlement, drove Tian Du out within months, killed the kings of Jiaodong and Jibei, and made himself king of a reunited Qi.
qi-206-bc.r: Qi became the main distraction that kept Xiang Yu from crushing Liu Bang. Xiang Yu invaded in 205 BCE and Tian Rong was killed, but Tian Heng rallied resistance and installed Tian Rong's son Tian Guang as king, with himself as chancellor. The kingdom rested on the loyalty of the Tian clan and the wealth of the Shandong coast.
qi-206-bc.e: In 203 BCE, as Liu Bang's envoy Li Yiji negotiated Qi's submission, Han Xin attacked anyway, routed the relief army of Long Ju on the Wei River and captured Tian Guang. Han Xin became King of Qi. Tian Heng fled to an island, where he and his followers killed themselves rather than submit.

qedarites.t: The most powerful Arab tribal confederation of the first millennium BCE, controlling desert routes from Syria to the oases of north Arabia.
qedarites.o: The Qedarites (biblical Kedar) appear in Assyrian records from the 8th century BCE as camel-herding Arabs of the Syrian desert and northern Arabia. Their centre was the oasis of Adummatu, modern Dumat al-Jandal, which held the shrine of their gods. Queen Zabibe paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, followed by Queen Samsi.
qedarites.r: They were led by kings and, unusually, by queens who also served as priestesses, among them Te'elhunu. The confederation controlled caravan routes carrying incense from south Arabia to the Levant and supplied camels and guides to imperial armies. Repeated revolts brought punitive campaigns: Sennacherib seized their idols, and Ashurbanipal fought Yauta son of Hazael in the 7th century BCE.
qedarites.e: Under the Achaemenid Empire the Qedarites kept their autonomy; Geshem the Arab, opponent of Nehemiah, and his son Qaynu, named king of Qedar on a silver bowl from Egypt, date to the 5th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE their place was taken by the Nabataean Kingdom.

qashqai-confederation.t: A Turkic-speaking confederation of nomadic tribes in Fars whose ilkhans were a major political force in southern Iran until exiled in 1954.
qashqai-confederation.o: The Qashqai are Turkic tribes who migrate seasonally between winter pastures near the Gulf and summer pastures in the Zagros north of Shiraz. They coalesced as a confederation in the 18th century, and under Karim Khan of the Zand Empire their chief Jani Agha rose to prominence. Fath Ali Shah of Qajar Iran recognised his son Jani Khan as ilkhan in 1818.
qashqai-confederation.r: The ilkhans ruled through tribal khans and kalantars, controlling migration routes, taxes and armed horsemen. Qashqai women are known for weaving gabbeh rugs and kilims. In the First World War Ismail Khan Solat al-Dowleh fought the British-led South Persia Rifles. Reza Shah forced the tribes to settle and Solat al-Dowleh died in prison in 1933.
qashqai-confederation.e: After 1941 his sons Naser Khan and Khosrow Khan revived Qashqai power and supported Mohammad Mosaddegh. After the 1953 coup they were exiled in 1954, ending the confederation's political autonomy; the Qashqai people remain a distinct community.

quirigua.t: A small Maya kingdom in the Motagua valley that won independence from Copán in 738 and raised the tallest carved stone monuments of the Maya world.
quirigua.o: Quiriguá was founded or refounded in 426 CE as a dependency of Copán, about 50 kilometres to the south, by agents of Copán's founder K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo'. It controlled the lower Motagua river, a route for jade and obsidian toward the Caribbean.
quirigua.r: Its ruler K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat was installed under Copán's authority in 724. In 738, probably backed by the Kingdom of Kaan, he captured and beheaded Copán's king Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, freeing Quiriguá. He celebrated with enormous sandstone stelae, including Stela E, over 10 metres tall, and zoomorphic boulders carved with long texts.
quirigua.e: Quiriguá prospered for several decades after its victory but its last monuments date to about 810, after which it declined. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

qi-huang-chao.t: The regime of the rebel Huang Chao, who seized Chang'an and declared himself emperor of Great Qi, dealing the Tang dynasty a blow from which it never recovered.
qi-huang-chao.o: Huang Chao, a salt smuggler who had failed the civil service examinations, joined Wang Xianzhi's rebellion in 875 and led it after Wang's death in 878. His army swept through southern China, sacking Guangzhou in 879, then turned north, took Luoyang and entered Chang'an at the start of 881, proclaiming himself emperor of Great Qi.
qi-huang-chao.r: Huang Chao set up a court with officials, reign titles and some surrendered Tang servants, while Emperor Xizong fled to Chengdu. But the regime controlled little beyond the capital region, food ran short, and executions of officials and massacres of the city's population turned the elite against it.
qi-huang-chao.e: His general Zhu Wen defected to the Tang in 882, and in 883 the Shatuo cavalry of Li Keyong drove Huang Chao from Chang'an. He fled east and was killed in 884 near Mount Tai. The Tang Dynasty survived only in name, as Zhu Wen and Li Keyong became the dominant warlords.

qasim-khanate.t: A Tatar vassal state created by Moscow on the Oka, whose Muslim khans served the Russian rulers for over two centuries.
qasim-khanate.o: In 1452 Vasily II of Moscow granted the town of Gorodets Meshchersky on the Oka, later renamed Kasimov, to Qasim, a son of Ulugh Muhammad, founder of the Khanate of Kazan, who had entered Moscow's service. It became a small Tatar khanate under Moscow's protection.
qasim-khanate.r: Its khans, descendants of Genghis Khan, ruled a Tatar nobility and local Meshchera and Russian subjects, kept their Muslim faith and served in Moscow's armies. Moscow used them as rival candidates for the throne of Kazan, and Shah Ali of Kasimov was installed there more than once. The khan's mosque and the tomb of Shah Ali still stand in Kasimov.
qasim-khanate.e: The khanate gradually lost its independence, and its later rulers converted to Christianity or were controlled by Moscow. After the death of the last ruler, Fatima Sultan, in 1681, it was abolished and absorbed into the Tsardom of Russia.

qaraunas.t: A Mongol military confederation of the Afghan borderlands, raiders of India and Persia who became kingmakers in the Chagatai lands.
qaraunas.o: The Qara'unas originated in Mongol garrison troops stationed in what is now Afghanistan in the mid-13th century, including contingents left by the general Negüder, after whom they were also called Negüderis. By the 1260s they formed an independent force in the region of Ghazni and Balkh.
qaraunas.r: They were a nomadic warrior confederation of mixed Mongol and Turkic origin, organised in tumens under their own commanders. They raided the Ilkhanate, Kerman and Fars, and launched repeated invasions of the Delhi Sultanate in the late 13th and early 14th centuries. They later formed a major component of the Chagatai Khanate's western forces.
qaraunas.e: Their leader Qazaghan dominated the Western Chagatai Khanate from 1346 until his murder in 1358. His grandson Amir Husayn was overthrown by Timur in 1370, and the Qara'unas were absorbed into the Timurid army.

quadi.t: A Suebian people north of the middle Danube who, with the Marcomanni, fought Rome under Marcus Aurelius and later joined the great migration into Spain.
quadi.o: The Quadi settled in Moravia and western Slovakia, probably moving there from the Main region around the same time as the Marcomanni at the end of the 1st century BCE. They formed part of the realm of Maroboduus and later of the client kingdom of Vannius, established by Rome in 19.
quadi.r: Ruled by kings, often confirmed by Rome, the Quadi lived in villages, traded with Roman Pannonia and buried their elite with Roman imports. They joined the Marcomannic Wars from 166; the 'Rain Miracle' depicted on the Column of Marcus Aurelius took place on their territory. Rome built forward posts in their land such as Mušov.
quadi.e: In 374 the killing of their king Gabinius by a Roman officer provoked a raid into Pannonia, and Emperor Valentinian I died in 375 while confronting their envoys. In 406 many Quadi crossed the Rhine with the Vandals and Alans, probably becoming part of the Suebian kingdom in Spain.

qatna.t: Qatna, a wealthy Bronze Age kingdom near Homs whose intact royal tomb and palace show Syria's prosperity between Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites.
qatna.o: Qatna, at Tell el-Mishrifeh, was refounded at the start of the 2nd millennium BCE inside huge square earthen ramparts. Its Amorite kings controlled central Syria and the caravan routes from the Euphrates to the coast, and became the main rivals of Yamhad.
qatna.r: In the Mari era King Ishhi-Addu allied with Shamshi-Adad and married his daughter to Yasmah-Addu. The royal palace held a hypogeum, found unplundered in 2002, with gold, ivory and the bones of generations of the royal family. Later kings left Akkadian archives with many Hurrian words.
qatna.e: In the 14th century BCE Qatna lay between the Mitanni Empire, the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and the Hittite Empire. Its king Akizzi appealed to Egypt in the Amarna letters, but Hittite forces under Suppiluliuma I sacked the city c. 1340 BCE and it never recovered.

qin-dynasty.t: China's first imperial dynasty, which unified the warring states in 221 BCE and imposed one script, one currency and one bureaucracy, then collapsed within fifteen years.
qin-dynasty.o: Between 230 and 221 BCE King Zheng of the State of Qin conquered the six rival states, the last being the State of Qi. He took the new title Huangdi, emperor, and is known as Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. His capital remained Xianyang in the Wei valley.
qin-dynasty.r: Advised by Li Si, the emperor abolished hereditary fiefs and divided the empire into 36, later more, commanderies run by appointed officials. Script, weights, measures, coinage and axle widths were standardised, roads and the Lingqu canal were built, and Meng Tian linked earlier walls against the Xiongnu. Harsh Legalist law, mass labour levies and the burning of books in 213 BCE bred resentment. The emperor's mausoleum was guarded by the Terracotta Army.
qin-dynasty.e: After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, Zhao Gao and Li Si installed his son Huhai as Second Emperor. Revolts led by Chen Sheng began in 209 BCE, and in 206 BCE the last ruler, Ziying, surrendered to Liu Bang. The Han Dynasty kept the Qin system of centralised imperial government.

qi-five-dynasties.t: The domain of the warlord Li Maozhen west of Chang'an, which stayed loyal to the memory of the Tang and refused to recognise the Later Liang.
qi-five-dynasties.o: Li Maozhen, born Song Wentong, rose as an officer in the imperial guard and became military governor of Fengxiang, west of Chang'an, in 887, receiving the imperial surname Li. He was made Prince of Qi in 901 and that year took Emperor Zhaozong into his custody until Zhu Wen's siege of Fengxiang forced him to hand him over in 903.
qi-five-dynasties.r: After the Tang fell in 907, Li Maozhen kept using the Tang reign era and the title Prince of Qi but never declared himself emperor. He ran a princely court with appointed officials. His domain shrank steadily as Former Shu took his southern prefectures, and he relied on alliances with the state of Jin (Five Dynasties).
qi-five-dynasties.e: When Li Cunxu destroyed the Later Liang and founded the Later Tang, Li Maozhen submitted in 924 and was confirmed as Prince of Qin. He died later that year, and his son Li Congyan succeeded him only as an ordinary provincial governor.

qara-khitai.t: A Khitan empire founded in Central Asia by refugees from the fallen Liao dynasty, whose defeat of the Seljuks inspired European legends of Prester John.
qara-khitai.o: When the Jurchen destroyed the Khitan Liao dynasty in northern China in 1125, the prince Yelü Dashi fled west with followers. He took Balasagun from the Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate around 1134, proclaimed himself gurkhan and founded the Western Liao, known as Qara Khitai.
qara-khitai.r: The gurkhans ruled a mostly Muslim population through vassal dynasties such as the Kara-Khanids, the Kingdom of Qocho and the Khwarazmshahs, collecting tribute instead of governing directly. The court kept Chinese-style titles and reign names while tolerating all religions. In 1141 Yelü Dashi crushed the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Qatwan steppe near Samarkand, news of which reached Europe as the legend of Prester John.
qara-khitai.e: In 1211 the Naiman prince Kuchlug, a refugee from Genghis Khan, seized the throne, persecuting Muslims. The Khwarazmian Empire took its western lands, and in 1218 Mongol forces under Jebe killed Kuchlug and absorbed Qara Khitai.
qara-khitai.re: Buddhism, Sunni Islam, Church of the East

qarmatians-of-bahrain.t: A radical Isma'ili state in eastern Arabia, ruled by a council at al-Ahsa, that stole the Black Stone from Mecca in 930.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.o: In 899 the missionary Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi, preaching the coming of the Mahdi, won over Bedouin and peasants in eastern Arabia, then called Bahrain, and took al-Ahsa and Qatif. His state broke with the Fatimid Caliphate's claims to leadership and became a separate Qarmatian power.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.r: After Abu Sa'id, the state was governed by a council of his descendants and leading men. Visitors such as Nasir Khusraw reported that citizens paid no taxes, debts were interest free and thousands of African slaves worked the date groves. Under Abu Tahir the Qarmatians raided Basra and Kufa, attacked pilgrim caravans and in 930 sacked Mecca, carrying the Black Stone to al-Ahsa until 951.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.e: Their power declined after defeats by the Fatimids and the Buyids and the loss of Oman. In 1077 Abd Allah al-Uyuni, a local chief, overthrew them with help from the Seljuk Empire and founded the Uyunid Emirate.

quitu-cara.t: The peoples of the Quito basin before the Incas, remembered in Ecuadorian tradition as the Kingdom of Quito ruled by the Shyris, a story many historians doubt.
quitu-cara.o: The Quitu were the inhabitants of the highland basin where Quito now stands, settled since at least the first millennium CE. In 1789 the Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco wrote that the Cara people came from the coast around 980 and founded a kingdom ruled by kings called Shyris, which united the northern highlands.
quitu-cara.r: Archaeology shows a landscape of local chiefdoms around Quito and its valleys, with farming of maize and potatoes and markets where goods from the coast and Amazon were traded. Velasco's account of a centralised kingdom with a line of Shyri kings has no support from earlier chronicles and is widely regarded as legend, though it became a cornerstone of Ecuadorian national identity.
quitu-cara.e: The Quito region fell to the Incas in the late 15th century and became their northern capital under Huayna Capac. After Atahualpa's capture, the Inca general Rumiñahui held Quito until the Spanish took it in 1534.

qaraqushs-tripolitania.t: The freebooting domain of Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush, an Ayyubid mamluk who carved out power in Tripolitania and southern Ifriqiya against the Almohads.
qaraqushs-tripolitania.o: Qaraqush, an Armenian mamluk in the service of Taqi al-Din, nephew of Saladin, led Turkish and Ghuzz soldiers west from Egypt around 1172. Exploiting Almohad weakness east of Tunis, he gathered support from Arab tribes and took towns in Tripolitania, the Jabal Nafusa and the region of Gabès, acting as an adventurer more than as an agent of the Ayyubid Empire.
qaraqushs-tripolitania.r: His power rested on a mobile army of Turkish soldiers and Bedouin allies rather than settled institutions. He allied at times with the Banu Ghaniya of Ifriqiya against the Almohad Caliphate, and the two sides' campaigns ravaged southern Tunisia and Tripolitania. Little is known of any administration beyond tribute and plunder.
qaraqushs-tripolitania.e: Qaraqush lost ground to Almohad counter-attacks and then quarrelled with his Banu Ghaniya allies. Yahya ibn Ghaniya captured and killed him around 1212 in the oases of the Fezzan region, and his followers dispersed.

quba-khanate.t: A khanate in north-eastern Azerbaijan whose ruler Fatali Khan united much of the eastern Caucasus in the late 18th century.
quba-khanate.o: The khanate grew out of the Quba district on the Caspian slope of the Caucasus. Its rulers, from a local family, were recognised by the Safavid Empire in 1726 and by Nader Shah, and after Nader's death in 1747 Husayn Ali Khan ruled as an effectively independent khan from his new town of Quba.
quba-khanate.r: Fatali Khan, who ruled from 1758, conquered the Derbent Khanate in 1765, dominated the Baku Khanate and the Javad Khanate and took Shamakhi, creating the largest state in the eastern Caucasus. He built a strong administration and army and negotiated with Catherine the Great. The khanate lived from farming, carpets, silk and Caspian trade.
quba-khanate.e: After Fatali Khan's death in 1789, his union fell apart. His son Sheikh Ali Khan resisted the Russian advance, but in 1806 the Russian Empire occupied Quba and Derbent and later abolished the khanate.

qarinvand-dynasty.t: A branch of the great Parthian noble house of Karen that ruled the mountains of Tabaristan for three centuries, until its last prince Mazyar rebelled against the Abbasids.
qarinvand-dynasty.o: The Karen were one of the seven great noble houses of Parthian and Sasanian Iran. According to Ibn Isfandiyar's history of Tabaristan, Khosrow I granted the descendants of Sukhra land in the mountains of Tabaristan around 550, after their service against the Hephthalites. The family held the highland district later called the 'Mountains of Qarin'.
qarinvand-dynasty.r: The Qarinvandids were local princes with the Persian title ispahbad or similar, ruling a Zoroastrian peasant society in the Alborz forests and valleys. After the Arab conquest they held out alongside the Dabuyid dynasty and the Bavand dynasty, paying tribute but keeping their faith. Vandad Hormozd led a revolt against the Abbasid Caliphate in the 780s, and his son Qarin continued the family's power.
qarinvand-dynasty.e: Mazyar ibn Qarin converted to Islam and served al-Ma'mun, but rebelled against the caliph al-Mu'tasim and the Tahirid dynasty in 839. He was captured and executed in Samarra in 840, ending the dynasty.
